title: Technological Sovereignty Requires Choice, Skills, and Support, Panelists Say During OSS EU
gist: At Open Source Summit Europe in Prague, a Linux Foundation panel argued European tech sovereignty means credible alternatives, operational skills and local support, not avoiding global providers. Panelists stressed that source access is not operational sovereignty, hardware remains a gap, and Europe lacks local firms to support mature open source such as OpenStack.

insights.claim: European organizations do not need to avoid global technology providers to be more sovereign, but they need credible alternatives and the skills to use them.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Sovereignty is framed as optionality, which favors portable and open stacks over exclusion of US hyperscalers.
insights.locator: European organizations do not need to avoid

insights.claim: The EU cloud sovereignty framework lists eight objectives, including legal and jurisdictional, data and AI, operational and supply-chain sovereignty, and the practical question is which dependencies an organization must be able to change or control.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Gives a checklist for procurement and architecture decisions.
insights.locator: During the panel, the EU cloud sovereignty framework

insights.claim: A joint statement during the panel said it is naive to believe a region of the world can be 100% sovereign; sovereignty is about building bridges and maintaining options, not retreating behind fortress walls.
insights.speaker: Stephen Sopko
insights.so_what: Policy realism: total self-sufficiency is not the goal.

insights.claim: Jonathan Bryce said the most valuable thing about open source is choice: using Azure or AWS may be fine if the organization retains other options, as with Kubernetes running on own infrastructure or commercial clouds.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bryce
insights.so_what: Portability layers like Kubernetes reduce lock-in without banning hyperscalers.
insights.quote: "The most valuable thing with open source is the choice," Bryce said.
insights.locator: The most valuable thing with open source

insights.claim: Paula Grzegorzewska noted an alternative is useful only when switching is practical, since moving between proprietary systems can demand substantial time and expertise, particularly for governments.
insights.speaker: Paula Grzegorzewska
insights.so_what: Switching cost, not availability of alternatives, determines real sovereignty.

insights.claim: Bryce said access to source code alone does not provide operational sovereignty; organizations must know how to run, secure and monitor their systems, a distinction he associated with OVH's approach.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bryce
insights.so_what: Skills and operations are the binding constraint on sovereignty.
insights.locator: Bryce said access to source code alone

insights.claim: Bryce said that in conversations around a Shanghai conference, China's sovereignty discussion focused less on open-source software and more on access to chips and optical systems, so software choice does not remove hardware dependencies.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bryce
insights.so_what: Hardware, not software, is the remaining sovereignty gap.

insights.claim: Thierry Carrez described proposed cloud and AI assurance levels varying by workload, with the highest requiring effective control over the full supply chain including hardware, and confidential computing as a way to limit host access when that is not required.
insights.speaker: Thierry Carrez
insights.so_what: Workload-tiered assurance could shape EU public procurement requirements.
insights.locator: Carrez described proposed cloud and AI assurance levels

insights.claim: Christopher Robinson linked sovereignty to security due diligence: open code and documentation let buyers examine vulnerability-response practices, and under the EU Cyber Resilience Act manufacturers bear substantial responsibility for products including their open-source components.
insights.speaker: Christopher "CRob" Robinson
insights.so_what: CRA liability pushes vendors to vet open-source dependencies.
insights.locator: Robinson linked sovereignty to security due diligence

insights.claim: Carrez noted the Cyber Resilience Act takes account of software assembled from many dependencies rather than treating it as a boxed product.
insights.speaker: Thierry Carrez
insights.so_what: The regulation acknowledges modern supply chains.

insights.claim: Open source is not simply a cheaper option: free code can start as an experiment and become a critical system needing sustained support.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Total cost includes long-term support capacity.
insights.locator: The panel also challenged the assumption

insights.claim: Carrez identified a shortage of local European companies able to package and support mature projects like OpenStack, citing Société Générale building expertise in-house for lack of a partner and the French Ministry of Finance seeking partners after its OpenStack deployment outgrew its scope.
insights.speaker: Thierry Carrez
insights.so_what: A market gap for European commercial support providers of open infrastructure.
insights.locator: Carrez identified a shortage of local companies

insights.claim: Carrez proposed investing in local service capabilities rather than rebuilding existing global projects, Grzegorzewska called for developer involvement in policymaking and investment alongside regulation, Robinson urged local expertise without isolationism, and Bryce argued broad contributor bases make projects more resilient.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Consensus favors funding services and skills over building European forks.
